newsitem.title: GERMANY: German state lets 16-year-olds vote on Sunday.
newsitem.headline: German state lets 16-year-olds vote on Sunday.

text.p: The German state of Lower Saxony holds local elections on Sunday after lowering the minimum voting age from 18 to 16.
Citizens of other European Union countries living in the northwestern state can also vote in the elections for mayors and local council members.
About 146,000 of the 6.2 million eligible voters are under the voting age of 18 years that is still the rule in other states and in national elections, poll officials say.

The vote, one of the few due to be held in Germany before the next general election in late 1998, will be watched as a barometer for national trends even though voters in such polls usually focus more on local issues.

The state's ruling Social Democrats (SPD) and the ecologist Greens backed a lower voting age for local elections after a 1994 opinion survey showed overwhelming youth support for their centre-left policies.

But more recent studies have shown first-time voters prefer Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU). Even in the university city Goettingen, one of the state's hotbeds of young radicals, the CDU runs ahead of the SPD in youth polls.

Although the SPD runs the state government, the CDU came out ahead in the last local polls in 1991 with 43.1 percent of the vote. The SPD scored 40.2 percent, the Greens 6.3 percent and the FDP 5.9 percent.
